overview:
Four years of fighting began when Confederate guns opened on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor in April 1861, though the rupture had come months earlier: Abraham Lincoln's election on a platform of halting slavery's expansion into the western territories prompted South Carolina to secede in December 1860, and ten more slave states followed by that June. The seceding states said plainly in their own declarations that the security of slavery was the cause; the Union initially fought only to restore itself. That changed as the war ground on. Enslaved people forced the issue by walking into Union lines in enormous numbers, Congress moved against slavery piecemeal, and on 1 January 1863 Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation declared free the enslaved in areas still in rebellion — a document that exempted loyal border states and Union-occupied territory, and whose promise depended entirely on armies making it real. It also opened the ranks: close to 200,000 Black men served in Union blue by 1865, roughly a tenth of the force.

Militarily the war divided into theaters that historians still argue about weighing. In the East, Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia fought Union armies to a bloody standstill through Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville before being checked at Antietam in 1862 and turned back at Gettysburg in July 1863. In the West, Ulysses S. Grant's capture of Vicksburg that same month split the Confederacy along the Mississippi, and William Tecumseh Sherman's campaigns through Georgia and the Carolinas in 1864–65 carried the war deliberately into the civilian economy that sustained Confederate armies. At sea a Union blockade slowly strangled Southern trade, and the duel of ironclads at Hampton Roads in 1862 was watched closely by every navy in Europe. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House in April 1865; scattered Confederate forces held out for weeks longer, and Lincoln was assassinated five days after Appomattox.

The war was not a self-contained American quarrel. Confederate strategy rested on the hope that British and French textile mills, starved of cotton, would force recognition and intervention — a gamble that failed as Britain found other suppliers and as emancipation made backing the South politically toxic. France used the distraction to install Maximilian on a throne in Mexico. And the conflict fell in the middle of a wider mid-century unmaking of forced labor: Russia emancipated its serfs in 1861, Cuba and Brazil would follow in the 1880s. Contemporaries on both sides of the Atlantic read the war as a test of whether a mass democracy could survive its own internal contradictions.
significance: The war settled by force two questions the American constitutional order had left open — whether states could leave the Union, and whether slavery could persist in it — and it did so at a cost that reshaped the country's demography, finances, and self-conception. Roughly four million people were freed, and the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments rewrote citizenship and the balance between federal and state power in ways still litigated today. It also left a South economically devastated and a settlement that Reconstruction's collapse largely undid for a century, while the mythology built afterward — the Lost Cause narrative that recast secession as a constitutional dispute rather than a defense of slavery — shaped monuments, textbooks, and politics far beyond the region. Militarily, its rifled weapons, entrenchments, railroads, telegraphy, ironclads, and deliberate targeting of civilian infrastructure are often read as a rehearsal for the industrialized wars of the following century.
coverage: Written from standard reference accounts (Britannica, Wikipedia), National Park Service and American Battlefield Trust figures, and the National Archives on the Emancipation Proclamation; the death toll is genuinely unsettled, with the traditional ~620,000 revised upward to ~750,000 by J. David Hacker in 2011 and to ~698,000 (±50,000) by a 2024 full-census study. The 516 events here are overwhelmingly battles and campaigns, which is also where the surviving record is densest — the dataset carries almost nothing on emancipation as a legal and lived process, the home fronts, guerrilla warfare in the border states, or the experience of the roughly four million enslaved people whose self-emancipation drove the war's course. Confederate records were heavily destroyed in the 1865 Richmond fire, and deaths among enslaved and freed people, refugees, and civilians were never systematically counted at all.
